claims.text: HashiCorp Vault is not open source; it is licensed under the Business Source License model.
Pulumi ESC is fully open source and licensed under Apache License 2.0.
HashiCorp Vault is licensed under Business Source License 1.1 and does not have an open source license.
Vault stores secrets only, whereas Pulumi ESC stores environments, secrets, and configurations.
Pulumi ESC environments can be composed together from multiple other environments, so shared configuration is inherited rather than duplicated.
Vault and Pulumi ESC differ in three fundamental ways: licensing, what they store, and composability.
Pulumi ESC environments can reference secrets stored in HashiCorp Vault.
Through Pulumi ESC, secrets stored in Vault can be organized as collections that are versioned, branched, and composed inside other collections.
Pulumi ESC can store non-secret configuration alongside secrets that are kept in Vault.
Pulumi ESC is a fully managed SaaS service provided by Pulumi Cloud.
Vault offers a hosted cloud service and self-hosting, and self-hosting Vault requires significant management overhead.
Both Pulumi ESC and Vault provide a key-value store.
Pulumi ESC supports pulling and using secrets from multiple sources including HashiCorp Vault, 1Password, and AWS Secrets Manager.
Vault can only store and manage secrets stored in Vault (it does not pull secrets from other sources).
Pulumi ESC supports both a GUI and a Document Editor with autocomplete, docs hover, and error checking.
Vault's UI offers a key/value form editor with a JSON toggle for editing secrets, and its editing and authoring capability is limited.
Pulumi ESC is available as `pulumi env` in the Pulumi CLI and supports injecting application secrets as environment variables and modifying secrets.
The `vault` CLI reads and writes secrets but does not inject them as environment variables.
Vault Agent's process supervisor mode injects secrets as environment variables (covering secret injection separately from the `vault` CLI).
Both Pulumi ESC and Vault provide client SDKs.

Pulumi ESC supports a declarative provider via the Pulumi Service Provider, which allows management (create, update, delete) of collections of secrets and configuration as a resource through infrastructure as code.
Individual Vault secrets can be managed as resources with the Vault provider for Pulumi or Terraform.
In Pulumi ESC, hierarchical environments inherit values from the environments they import.
Vault has no equivalent concept to hierarchical, composable environments; secrets are organized by path convention and the structure is maintained by hand.
Pulumi ESC values can be either secret or plaintext, whereas Vault values can only be secrets.
Pulumi ESC lets users see existing secrets, whereas Vault does not offer the ability to see existing secrets.
In Pulumi ESC, environments can import secrets from another environment, and secrets updated in the referenced environment automatically propagate to downstream environments.
Vault has no equivalent to Pulumi ESC secret referencing; Vault has no first-class environment to reference, so secrets are read by path.
Pulumi ESC can construct new dynamic values through string interpolation, whereas Vault cannot interpolate values from other values.
Pulumi ESC environments can be forked for testing without rewriting entire environments and overriding specific values; Vault does not support branching or personal configs.
`pulumi env diff` shows the changes between two environments or two versions of a single environment; Vault has no equivalent for comparing secrets across environments.
Pulumi ESC supports built-in functions such as `toJSON`, `fromJSON`, `fromBase64`, and `toString`, which allow data manipulation for any scenario.
Vault provides templating and transformation functions, such as username templating and the Transform secrets engine.
Vault does not provide functions for composing configuration values (in the way Pulumi ESC built-in functions do).
Both Pulumi ESC and Vault provide audit logs.
Pulumi ESC uses TLS for encryption in transit and unique encryption keys per environment for encryption at rest.
Vault uses a security barrier for all requests made to the backend, which automatically encrypts all data leaving Vault using a 256-bit AES cipher in Galois Counter Mode (GCM) with 96-bit nonces.
Pulumi ESC uses OIDC flows to generate dynamic credentials, available for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.
Vault cloud secrets engines generate short-lived credentials for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.
Each Vault cloud secrets engine is configured with a static credential that Vault uses to mint the short-lived credentials.
Pulumi Cloud can be used as an OIDC provider from the Pulumi SDK, CLI, UI, and `pulumi-service` provider.
Configuring Vault as an OIDC provider is only available from the CLI.
